Mitosis. The phase of the cell cycle in which the nucleus divides, producing two genetically identical daughter nuclei, each receiving a complete copy of the parent cell's chromosomes. The hallmark of somatic cell division, mitosis enables growth, repair, and asexual reproduction. It occurs in four classical stages—prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase—and is preceded by DNA replication and followed by cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm.

It's part of M phase, preceded by interphase during which DNA replicates in S phase and cells accumulate resources for division. Prophase begins when chromatin condenses into chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. The nuclear envelope breaks down, and the spindle apparatus forms from centrosomes at the poles. Metaphase follows as chromosomes align at the cell's equatorial plate. Spindle fibers attached to kinetochores are under tension, ensuring proper segregation.

Anaphase is when sister chromatids separate as spindle fibers shorten. Chromatids move to opposite poles, and the centromere splits, so each chromatid becomes an independent chromosome. Telophase concludes the process. Nuclear envelopes reform around the separated chromosome sets at each pole. Chromosomes decondense, and the spindle apparatus disappears. This produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells from one parent cell, each receiving a complete genome copy, ensuring genetic continuity.

The entire process takes roughly one to two hours in mammalian cells, with prophase taking about twenty minutes, metaphase about five minutes, anaphase about ten minutes, and telophase about fifteen minutes. Most of the cell cycle time—eighteen to twenty hours—is actually spent in interphase. Mitosis occurs in all eukaryotes. Centrioles organize spindle poles in animal cells and some plants, though plant spindle poles lack centrioles but form functional spindles anyway.

Checkpoint controls verify DNA integrity. The G1/S and G2/M checkpoints allow the p53 protein to detect damage and halt progression. Failure causes genomic instability and cancer. Cytokinesis follows mitosis: animal cells form a cleavage furrow through actin ring contraction, while plant cells form a cell plate, building a new cell wall.
